questions.question: What is a path in a metric space $(\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})$?
When is a path $\boldsymbol{p}$ called a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$?
In Euclidean space, what is the standard straight-line path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ given?
For $\boldsymbol{p}(t) = (\cos(2\pi t),\sin(2\pi t))$, what are the endpoints?
What is path concatenation used for?
options: Turning every discontinuous function into a continuous path
Constructing a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{c}$ from a path $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ and a path $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{c}$

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$, what is the reverse path given?
If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{c}$, what does concatenation produce?
If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$, what are the endpoints of $\boldsymbol{r}(t) = \boldsymbol{p}(1-t)$?
Why is continuity essential for a path?
options: A path is meant to be a continuous journey without jumps.
Continuity removes the need for endpoints.
Continuity means the domain must be $\boldsymbol{X}$ rather than $[0,1]$.

questions.question: Which condition is missing if a map $\boldsymbol{p}\colon[0,1]\to\boldsymbol{X}$ has the right endpoints but has a jump?
A map $p:[0,1]\to E$ satisfies $p(0)=a$ and $p(1)=b$, but it is not continuous. Why does it fail to be a path from $a$ to $b$?
options: A path must always be a straight line.
A path may not have prescribed endpoints.
A path must be defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
Continuity of $p$ is part of the definition of a path.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a path from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$, which formula defines a path from $\boldsymbol{b}$ to $\boldsymbol{a}$?
What is a path in a metric space $\boldsymbol X$?
When is $\boldsymbol p$ a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$?
options: When $\boldsymbol p(0)=\boldsymbol b$ and $\boldsymbol p(1)=\boldsymbol b$ only.
When $\boldsymbol p(0)=\boldsymbol a$ and $\boldsymbol p(1)=\boldsymbol b$.

questions.question: What does the interpretation of a path emphasise?
options: A continuous journey whose image stays in the space.
A discontinuous jump between two points, regardless of the specific input chosen.
A finite subcover of the space.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, which formula gives a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$?
options: $\boldsymbol p(t)=\boldsymbol b$ for all $t \lt 1$ and undefined at $1$

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol p$ is a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$, what is the reverse path?
If $\boldsymbol p$ is a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$ and $\boldsymbol q$ is a path from $\boldsymbol b$ to $\boldsymbol c$, what can be constructed?
options: A path from $\boldsymbol c$ to $\boldsymbol c$ only.
A discontinuous function from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$.
A metric with no triangle inequality.
A path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol c$.

questions.question: What kind of jump does continuity rule out for a path?
options: It prevents arbitrary jumps and makes the path a continuous curve in the space.
It forces the metric space to be compact, no matter which values are selected.
